title: Colour on a budget

open.what: Rerun on the pixel tidepool knocks on a shell: knock, knock, hollow. The open is silent.

close.what: Back on the tidepool, Rerun's glass shell throws its one spectral flare; it looks at the viewer and the film ends.

segments.heading: Colour on a budget
lines: Colour on a budget.

segments.heading: The budget
lines: In 1987, an IBM PC with VGA graphics had a mode of 320 by 200 pixels, one byte each.
A byte holds 256 values, so the screen showed 256 colours at once, each one picked from a palette of 262,144.

predict.question: A photograph has thousands of colours. Which 256 would you keep?

segments.heading: Choosing the 256
lines: In 1982, Paul Heckbert described a way to choose them, called median cut.
Put every colour in the picture into a box. Cut the box in two at the median of its longest side, and keep cutting the biggest piece until there are 256 boxes.
Each box becomes one palette colour, and each colour stands for about the same number of pixels.
He found pictures could drop to 8 bits per pixel with little visible loss.

segments.heading: The wrong fix
lines: When a smooth sky turns into stripes, the obvious fix is more colours. There is another way: keep the error, and spread it where the eye will average it out.

segments.heading: Ordered dither
lines: In 1973, B. E. Bayer published a pattern for this. Compare each pixel with a threshold from a small grid that repeats across the image.
With an 8 by 8 grid, black and white alone can show 65 levels of grey.

segments.heading: Error diffusion
lines: In the mid-1970s, Floyd and Steinberg passed each pixel's rounding error on to the neighbours still to be drawn.
Seven sixteenths go to the right. Three, five and one sixteenths go to the row below.
The noise is fine enough that the eye blends it back into the colour that was meant.

segments.heading: Blue noise
lines: A third way uses a grid of thresholds spread out evenly, built by Robert Ulichney's void-and-cluster method.
It reads as fine grain instead of a pattern.

segments.heading: Choosing in the right space
lines: Which palette colour is nearest depends on how you measure. raw-native measures in Oklab, a colour space designed so that equal steps look roughly equal.

segments.heading: In both engines
lines: raw-native's dither pass runs on the graphics card. For two palettes, it picks the same colour as the slow reference for every one of 16,777,216 colours.
BRender, from 1998, kept its textures the same way: each texel is an 8-bit index into a 256-colour palette.

segments.heading: Two things to keep
lines: Two things to keep. Pick the colours where the pixels are. Spend the error where the eye averages it away.
The voice you heard is a synthesized version of mine. Every number on screen links to its source under the video.
